clue.text: Foremost of humorists, or superb satirist

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of humorists
taken as written
ace as an adjective means excellent, superb

explanation.surface: The finest of the comic writers, or a brilliant satirist, is being praised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'superb satirist' reads as one phrase, but superb is wordplay and satirist alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace was the Roman poet whose Satires made him one of the founding figures of verse satire.

clue.text: Lively nightclubs, places of potential violence

blocks.note: first meaning: popular, buzzing places of entertainment
second meaning: areas where trouble or fighting is likely to flare up

explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the two parts one description of rough clubs; they are separate senses of the same phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used both for fashionable lively venues and for danger zones where conflict could break out.

clue.text: Machine in part of plant beginning to blacken within

blocks.note: the root is the underground part of a plant
the first letter of blacken

explanation.surface: A machine inside a greenhouse plant is starting to turn black.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter goes into the middle of ROOT: RO-B-OT.
explanation.definitionFit: A robot is an automatic machine that carries out tasks, often in place of a person.

clue.text: Foolish old man snatching her cigar

blocks.note: an old coot is a foolish or eccentric old man
taken as written

explanation.surface: A silly old man grabs a woman's cigar from her.
explanation.walkthrough: An old coot is a dated insult for a doddery, foolish old man; the bird is known for its bald-looking white forehead.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheroot is a cigar with both ends cut square, so it is a kind of cigar.

clue.text: Sword wound — one male found with it inside

taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: S(I M IT)CAR: the three small pieces sit together between the S and CAR of the wound word.
explanation.definitionFit: A scimitar is a curved single-edged sword of Middle Eastern origin.

clue.text: US politician, trickster entertaining Greek on English ship

standard abbreviation for Greek

explanation.walkthrough: The trickster word is split between its two halves to take the guests, rather than having them placed at one end.

clue.text: Wise man's headgear held by mother

explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay rather than marking possession. HAT sits in the middle of MAMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahatma, meaning great soul, is an Indian title of reverence for a sage, as in Mahatma Gandhi.

clue.text: Great Dane is barking in open-air restaurant

blocks.note: the letters of the dog breed

explanation.walkthrough: Barking looks like the dog's noise, but it is slang for barking mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea garden is an outdoor place where tea and light refreshments are served to customers.

clue.text: Bit of sunlight round end of December — it's an unusual thing

round means encircling, so the beam of light goes around the following pieces

blocks.note: a ray is a single beam of sunlight
the last letter of December
taken as written

explanation.surface: A glimpse of sun around late December is a rare event.
explanation.walkthrough: R and IT go between the RA and Y of RAY. The 's after it stands for 'is', linking to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rarity is something seldom found or seen, an uncommon thing.

clue.text: Pill, first to take on board

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter of the next word is used

the first letter of take

explanation.surface: A doctor tells a patient which pill to swallow first, or a team takes a pill on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take on board' reads as the idiom for accepting something; it is split into a letter source and a piece meaning table.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablet is a small compressed solid dose of medicine, the same thing as a pill.

clue.text: Going about, undecided

blocks.note: first meaning: circulating, as a rumour or feeling spreads around
second meaning: still unsettled, with plans not yet fixed

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'there's something in the air' covers the first sense; 'plans are still in the air' covers the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes both a mood or rumour that is widely felt and a matter that remains unresolved.

clue.text: Panda alarming pal with carrot

blocks.note: the letters of pal and carrot together

explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a panda, short for panda car, is a police vehicle used for routine patrols.

clue.text: New form of heroin (smack) for addict

explanation.definitionFit: A chain-smoker lights one cigarette from the last without pause, a compulsive smoker.

clue.text: Quirk admitted by orchestra (I think)

explanation.definitionFit: A quirk is an odd personal characteristic, and a trait is any distinguishing characteristic.

clue.text: Transmit Hardy's novel novel

explanation.definitionFit: Tristram Shandy is Laurence Sterne's famously digressive eighteenth-century comic novel.

clue.text: Everyone I upset and make fun of is uncomfortable

taken as written
to tease is to make fun of someone

explanation.definitionFit: To be ill at ease is to feel awkward or uneasy, which is being uncomfortable.

clue.text: British poet in game reportedly being broadcast

a programme that is on is being broadcast

explanation.surface: A poet appears in a sports programme being shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: Said together, the pieces sound like 'tennis on', as when Wimbledon is on the TV.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate who wrote In Memoriam and The Charge of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: Like Jean Harlow double in plant, upset about bit of mimicry

the first letter of mimicry

explanation.surface: A film star's body double is planted on set, upset at being mimicked.
explanation.walkthrough: The thirteen jumbled letters wrap around the single letter from mimicry.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Harlow, the 1930s Hollywood star, was nicknamed the Platinum Blonde for her near-white hair, after her 1931 film of that title.

clue.text: Inform one about piece of rope on second latticework structure

the Roman numeral for one
the first letter of rope
standard abbreviation for second

clue.text: Ill-fated lover, chief around the North

N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.definitionFit: Leander, lover of Hero in Greek myth, drowned swimming to her, so he is a classic doomed lover.

clue.text: Secret cupboard

blocks.note: the last letter of drill
standard abbreviation for Italian
the male pronoun
